issues.legal_issue: An interim prohibition on mining must remain in force until a monitoring committee has examined the affected mines and its report has been considered.
material_facts: Expert reports and site inspections recorded extensive environmental degradation, groundwater depletion, and widespread non-compliance with mining safeguards.

The court considered whether mining should resume immediately subject to safeguards or whether a monitoring committee should first inspect individual mines and report on whether resumption was appropriate.
The court selected the latter course as the safer response to the environmental risks.
issues.conclusion: The mining prohibition could not be vacated or varied before the monitoring committee’s report was considered.
issues.legal_principle: The precautionary principle requires anticipatory measures to prevent environmental harm and does not require direct proof of harm; where there is doubt, environmental protection takes precedence over economic interests. The court relied on Article 21, Articles 48-A and 51-A of the Constitution, Principle 15 of the Rio Conference, Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar, M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) 4 SCC 463, Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India, and A.P. Pollution Control Board v. Prof. M.V. Nayudu. It also relied on the findings and recommendations of NEERI, EPCA, CEC, and CMPDI.

rule.if: challenge_to_interim_mining_ban and (expert_reports_show_environmental_degradation or mining_safeguards_were_not_complied_with) and committee_inspection_is_needed

predicates.challenge_to_interim_mining_ban: A proceeding seeks to vacate or vary an interim prohibition on mining.
predicates.expert_reports_show_environmental_degrad: Expert reports or inspections identify environmental degradation or risks associated with the mining activity.
predicates.mining_safeguards_were_not_complied_with: The record shows that safeguards imposed for mining were not complied with.
predicates.committee_inspection_is_needed: The court determines that a committee should inspect individual mines and report before resumption is considered.

issues.definition: When an interim mining prohibition is challenged and the record shows environmental degradation or non-compliance, the prohibition remains until a needed committee report is considered.

issues.legal_issue: Environmental clearance is required when a mining lease is renewed after the environmental-clearance notification takes effect, even if the original lease predates the notification.
material_facts: Some mining leases had been granted before the notification requiring environmental clearance, while others were granted afterward.
Renewal of many leases came up for consideration after the notification, but the required environmental impact assessment clearance had not been obtained.
The notification required clearance before mining operations could be undertaken, and the court found that the renewal was a fresh grant.
issues.conclusion: The environmental-clearance notification applies to renewals considered after it took effect, and mining operations cannot commence without the required clearance.
issues.legal_principle: The notification dated 27 January 1994, issued under Sections 3(1) and 3(2)(v) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986, requires clearance for covered mining projects before operations commence. A renewal is a fresh grant and must comply with the law then in force. The court relied on Ambica Quarry Works v. State of Gujarat, Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P., and State of M.P. v. Krishnadas Tikaram; it distinguished Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India, which did not decide the application of the notification at the renewal stage.

predicates.mining_lease_renewal_is_considered: An authority is considering renewal of a mining lease.
predicates.clearance_requirement_is_in_force: A requirement for environmental clearance applies to the mining project when renewal is considered.
predicates.environmental_clearance_is_absent: The required environmental clearance has not been obtained.

issues.definition: When a mining lease is renewed under an applicable clearance requirement and clearance is absent, mining cannot commence without that clearance.

issues.legal_issue: Mining on land treated as forest in government records and affidavits requires prior approval for non-forestry use.
material_facts: The State Forest Department’s records treated the relevant leased areas as forest.
The State had filed affidavits treating the areas as forest and had sought central approval to use such land for non-forestry purposes.
The State later argued that the areas were not forest, but the court would not permit it to reverse its earlier position in the proceedings.
issues.conclusion: For purposes of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, the relevant areas must be treated as forest, and mining there for non-forestry purposes requires prior approval under that Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2 of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 restricts use of forest land for non-forest purposes without prior approval of the Central Government. In T.N. Godavarman Thirumulkpad v. Union of India, the court held that “forest” includes areas understood in the dictionary sense and areas recorded as forest in government records, irrespective of ownership. The court did not decide the independent legal effect of notifications under the Punjab Land Preservation Act, 1900; it relied on the government records, affidavits, and conduct in this case.

predicates.mining_is_proposed_on_land_for_non_fores: Mining is proposed on land for a purpose other than forestry.
predicates.government_records_treat_land_as_forest: Government records or formal government representations treat the land as forest.

issues.definition: If mining for non-forestry use is proposed on land treated as forest in government records, prior approval for that use is required.

issues.legal_issue: Mining is prohibited on land planted under a publicly funded ecological restoration project.
material_facts: The Aravalli project involved extensive afforestation and ecological restoration, with substantial foreign funding.
Mining leases had been granted over areas where plantations had been undertaken under that project.
The court rejected the argument that mining should be excluded only from the specific portion where plantation damage had occurred.
issues.conclusion: No mining activity can be carried out on areas where plantation was undertaken under the Aravalli project using foreign funds.
issues.legal_principle: The court relied on the National Forest Policy, 1988, the ecological value of the restored land, and the need to protect forest and environmental assets. It held that permitting mining on such project areas would be arbitrary, unreasonable, and illogical, and rejected selective exclusion of only the portion directly damaged by mining.

predicates.mining_lease_covers_project_restoration_: A mining lease includes land used for an ecological restoration project.
predicates.project_land_was_planted_with_external_f: Plantation on the project land was undertaken using external funding.

issues.definition: If a mining lease covers land planted as part of an externally funded ecological restoration project, mining is prohibited on that project land.

issues.legal_issue: Mining may be permitted only on a sustainable-development basis and subject to stringent safeguards and compliance.
material_facts: The reports described serious effects of mining on ecology, land, air quality, and groundwater, as well as failures to enforce existing safeguards.
The court recognized the need for development, employment, and revenue, but concluded that these interests did not justify irreversible environmental harm.

The court directed that mining be considered on an individual-mine basis after inspection and implementation of expert recommendations, and stated that violations could put a lease at risk of cancellation.
issues.conclusion: Mining may be permitted only on the basis of sustainable development and compliance with stringent conditions; violations risk cancellation of the lease.
issues.legal_principle: Article 21 protects the right to enjoy pollution-free water and air; Article 48-A directs the State to protect and improve the environment, and Article 51-A imposes a corresponding duty on citizens. The court applied sustainable development, the precautionary principle, and the polluter-pays principle, relying on M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) 4 SCC 463, Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India, and A.P. Pollution Control Board v. Prof. M.V. Nayudu. It also relied on the statutory environmental safeguards under the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960, and the Mineral Conservation and Development Rules, 1988.

rule.if: mining_is_proposed and mining_creates_environmental_risk and safeguards_can_protect_environment and compliance_is_monitored

predicates.mining_is_proposed: A party proposes to undertake mining activity.
predicates.mining_creates_environmental_risk: The proposed mining presents a risk of harm to the environment or human health.
predicates.safeguards_can_protect_environment: Safeguards are available that can reduce or prevent the environmental harm while permitting mining.
predicates.compliance_is_monitored: Compliance with the safeguards is subject to monitoring.

issues.definition: Where proposed mining poses environmental risks, it may be permitted only if safeguards can protect the environment and compliance is monitored.

issues.legal_issue: The monitoring committee must examine minor-mineral leases for environmental risks even though the environmental-clearance notification does not apply to them.
material_facts: Some leases concerned extraction of minor minerals.
The court found that minor-mineral mining could also cause significant harm, particularly when mines operated in clusters.
The court expressly noted that the 1994 environmental-clearance notification did not apply to those leases.
issues.conclusion: The monitoring committee must examine minor-mineral leases in light of the environmental risks and report on them, while recognizing that the 1994 notification does not apply to those leases.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the precautionary approach and required risks of harm to the environment or human health to be assessed in the public interest under the reasonable-person test. It relied on CMPDI’s report and the environmental principles discussed in A.P. Pollution Control Board v. Prof. M.V. Nayudu; it expressly distinguished the committee’s review from application of the 1994 environmental-clearance notification.

predicates.minor_mineral_mining_lease_is_under_revi: A lease for extraction of minor minerals is under review.
predicates.environmental_risk_requires_assessment: The mining activity presents environmental risks that require assessment.

issues.definition: When a minor-mineral lease is under review and environmental risks require assessment, the monitoring committee must examine it and report.

issues.legal_issue: The environmental safeguards recommended by experts must be applied to mining in the second affected district, and the prohibition there cannot be lifted before mine-specific review.
material_facts: The principal CMPDI study concerned mining in one district, but its general safeguards and recommendations addressed environmental problems also present in the other district.
The court directed the monitoring committee to inspect the leases in the other district and report on whether mining should recommence.
The court stated that lifting the prohibition before implementation of expert recommendations and consideration of the committee’s mine-specific report would not be expedient.
issues.conclusion: The general safeguards and recommendations must be implemented in the other district, and the mining prohibition should not be lifted before the committee reports on individual leases.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the precautionary principle and sustainable development, relying on the recommendations of NEERI, EPCA, CEC, and CMPDI, as well as the environmental and public-health principles set out under Article 21 and related constitutional provisions. It held that safeguards developed for one affected area could appropriately be applied to the other in the public interest.

predicates.mining_prohibition_is_in_force: A prohibition on mining is in force in the area under consideration.
predicates.expert_findings_show_comparable_environm: Expert findings identify environmental risks comparable to those addressed by safeguards developed for another affected area.
predicates.mine_specific_review_is_pending: A monitoring committee has not yet completed its review of individual leases.

issues.definition: When a mining prohibition is in force, comparable environmental risks have been identified, and mine-specific review is pending, the prohibition remains until the report is considered.

issues.legal_issue: Mining that reaches the groundwater table may not continue in the affected area.
material_facts: Groundwater reports found that dewatering mines affected groundwater levels and depleted groundwater resources in the mine areas and surrounding buffer zones.
Inspections found deep pits containing groundwater and pumps or pipes used to remove water so mining could continue.
The leaseholders agreed that the monitoring committee would identify areas where the groundwater level had been reached and that they would not mine in those areas.
issues.conclusion: The monitoring committee must exclude areas where mining has reached the groundwater level, and mining must not be undertaken there.
issues.legal_principle: The court relied on the groundwater-related conditions in mining clearances, the Central Ground Water Board’s findings, and the precautionary principle. It accepted the leaseholders’ agreement that areas where groundwater was reached would be carved out and not mined.

predicates.mining_reaches_groundwater_level: Mining operations reach the groundwater level in the area being mined.
predicates.mining_area_is_under_monitoring_review: The mining area is subject to review by a monitoring body.

issues.definition: If mining reaches the groundwater level in an area under monitoring review, mining is prohibited in that affected area.

issues.legal_issue: An administrative circular cannot extend the environmental-clearance deadline so as to authorize mining undertaken without the clearance required by the statutory notification.
material_facts: Mining activity had been undertaken without the environmental clearance required by the 1994 notification.
A ministry circular extended the opportunity for defaulting units to seek clearance after commencing activity.
The court found that the circular did not purport to legalize mining without compliance and, in any event, could not alter the statutory notification.
issues.conclusion: The circular does not apply to mining activity and cannot authorize commencement or continuation of mining without the required clearance.
issues.legal_principle: The 1994 notification, issued under Sections 3(1) and 3(2)(v) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986, is mandatory. A statutory notification cannot be modified by an administrative circular, and the clearance requirement must be satisfied before covered mining commences.

predicates.mining_began_without_required_clearance: Mining activity began without a clearance required by an applicable environmental rule.
predicates.administrative_circular_is_relied_on_to_: An administrative circular is relied on as authority to cure the failure to obtain that clearance.

issues.definition: If mining began without required clearance, an administrative circular relied on to cure that failure does not authorize the mining.
